articles.body: Services Top Right Summit Shipping announces new China–Red Sea container service November 14, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Summit Singapore; Source:VesselFinder Summit Shipping Line has announced the launch of its new China Red Sea Service (CRS), establishing a weekly container shipping connection between China and three major Red Sea ports, according to DynaLiners. The Singapore-based carrier plans to deploy eight dedicated container vessels, each with a capacity of approximately 2,000 TEU, to support the new service. According to the company’s latest announcement, the CRS service will follow the port rotation: Shanghai – Ningbo – Nansha – Jeddah – Aqaba – Sokhna – Shanghai. The service will connect the Chinese export gateways of Shanghai, Ningbo and Nansha with Jeddah in Saudi Arabia, Aqaba in Jordan and Sokhna in Egypt. With eight vessels operating on a weekly rotation, Summit Shipping aims to provide regular container capacity between China and the Red Sea region. The new connection will expand the carrier’s regional service network, adding direct coverage between major Chinese ports and Red Sea markets. Summit Shipping has not specified the first sailing date or identified the vessels assigned to the service in its latest announcement. articles.body: Services Top Right Evergreen and RCL join Emirates Shipping’s new East Africa service November 14, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Evergreen container ships at Terminal 7 of Kaohsiung Port Evergreen and Regional Container Lines (RCL) will participate in the new Far East–East Africa container service alongside Emirates Shipping Line and Interasia Lines, with the four carriers marketing the connection under separate service brands. According to shipping intelligence provider Linerlytica, the service will operate as FAX2 for Emirates Shipping Line, AEF6 for Evergreen, EA3 for Interasia Lines and REA3 for RCL. The service will connect three major Chinese ports with Mombasa, Kenya, through Malaysia’s Port Klang. The full port rotation will be: Qingdao – Ningbo – Nansha – Port Klang – Mombasa – Qingdao. The first sailing is scheduled to depart Qingdao on 5 December 2026. According to Linerlytica, the service will deploy seven container vessels ranging from 2,700 to 4,200 TEU, operating on a 49-day rotation. The first scheduled vessel is the 2,824 TEU HIRANYA BHUM. Emirates Shipping Line had previously announced the FAX2 service as part of its expansion of connections between Asia and East Africa. The additional carrier participation establishes the wider commercial arrangement supporting the new route to Mombasa. articles.title: MOVe Logistics adds Newcastle to trans-Tasman shipping service
articles.summary: New Zealand-based MOVe Logistics has expanded its trans-Tasman multipurpose shipping service with a call at Newcastle, Australia, strengthening connections between regional ports in the two countries. The expanded service commenced operations at Newcastle on 27 October 2026, when the multipurpose vessel Brio Faith...
articles.body: New Zealand-based MOVe Logistics has expanded its trans-Tasman multipurpose shipping service with a call at Newcastle, Australia, strengthening connections between regional ports in the two countries. The expanded service commenced operations at Newcastle on 27 October 2026, when the multipurpose vessel Brio Faith called at the port’s Mayfield Multipurpose Terminal carrying containers and breakbulk cargo. The monthly service is operated by the 9,000 dwt Brio Faith, which has a container carrying capacity of approximately 630 TEU and is equipped with two 40-tonne cranes for handling breakbulk and project cargo. In addition to Newcastle, the service covers Marsden Point, Tauranga, Lyttelton, Dunedin and Bluff in New Zealand, alongside Bell Bay, Brisbane, Townsville and Port Alma in Australia. The operation accommodates containerised shipments, breakbulk, out-of-gauge cargo and specialised project shipments, providing transport options for manufacturers, exporters and importers across the Tasman Sea. According to the Port of Newcastle, the new connection offers businesses in the Hunter region an alternative to moving international cargo through Sydney’s ports, potentially reducing inland transportation costs and congestion-related delays. MOVe Logistics has operated its trans-Tasman shipping network since 2022, focusing on regional ports and cargo types that require flexible handling arrangements. The addition of Newcastle expands the service’s Australian coverage and provides another maritime connection for New South Wales businesses trading with New Zealand.

articles.summary: All passengers and crew aboard an American Cruise Lines riverboat survived after a Marshall Islands-flagged asphalt tanker struck the docked paddle-wheeler on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday,...

REUTERS/Christiana Botic TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY All passengers and crew aboard an American Cruise Lines riverboat survived after a Marshall Islands-flagged asphalt tanker struck the docked paddle-wheeler on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, causing it to capsize and sending people into the water. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed that everyone aboard the American Heritage had been accounted for following a massive rescue operation. Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals, including 30 passengers and two police officers, but none suffered critical injuries. “We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said at a news conference. The 160-meter tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the U.S.-flagged American Heritage at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time as it was traveling upbound on the Lower Mississippi River, just below the Crescent City Connection bridge, according to the Port of New Orleans. Video of the collision shows the much larger tanker striking the docked paddlewheeler, which began taking on water and listing heavily before eventually capsizing alongside the dock. Other footage shows people in the river wearing life jackets as tugboat operators, nearby vessel crews, police and emergency responders rushed to pull them to safety. The American Heritage had docked outside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building approximately two hours earlier to begin disembarking passengers following an eight-day Mississippi River cruise. Port officials initially reported approximately 129 passengers aboard, in addition to crew members. Moreno said passengers began evacuating after the initial impact, but the vessel overturned before everyone could get off, forcing rescuers to pull people from the water. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry praised the response, calling the outcome “nothing short of a miracle.” “While we will continue to work through the details of this incident, one thing is clear: our first responders on the national, state, and local level saved countless lives today, and for that I and all of our country are thankful!” Landry said. In an updated statement Friday, American Cruise Lines said it was arranging hotel accommodations and assistance for everyone who had been aboard the American Heritage . “We are getting everyone who was aboard the ship settled into hotels and making sure they have everything they need,” the company said. American Cruise Lines also thanked the U.S. Coast Guard, its crew and local first responders for their rescue efforts, adding that it remained in close contact with the Coast Guard, New Orleans Police and other agencies. The cause of the collision remains under investigation, although the U.S. Coast Guard said the tanker may have experienced a steering failure. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said the tanker appeared to have experienced “some type of loss of steering,” but emphasized that the exact cause had not been determined. The National Transportation Safety Board has launched an investigation and is sending a team to New Orleans, with investigators expected to arrive Saturday morning. The Coast Guard also closed the Mississippi River to vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 while emergency operations continued, temporarily disrupting navigation along one of the nation’s busiest commercial waterways. Officials said they were evaluating when the waterway could safely reopen. According to MarineTraffic , the Atlantic Asphalt is a 160-meter asphalt and bitumen tanker sailing under the Marshall Islands flag. The American Heritage is an 81-meter U.S.-flagged paddlewheel cruise ship built in 2015 with accommodations for up to 150 passengers. AIS data shows the Atlantic Asphalt called at Amuay, Venezuela, in October before arriving in Paulsboro, New Jersey. The tanker departed Paulsboro on October 26 and arrived in New Orleans on November 11, two days before the collision. The investigation will focus on what caused the tanker to strike the docked passenger vessel along the busy Lower Mississippi River, where deep-draft oceangoing ships regularly navigate in close proximity to river cruise vessels, tugs and barges. articles.title: Aliança shifts ALCT1 service from Sepetiba to Rio de Janeiro
articles.summary: Aliança, Maersk’s Brazilian shipping subsidiary, will replace its existing Sepetiba call with Rio de Janeiro on its domestic cabotage ALCT1 service, effective from 4 December 2026. articles.body: Aliança, Maersk’s Brazilian shipping subsidiary, will replace its existing Sepetiba call with Rio de Janeiro on its domestic cabotage ALCT1 service, effective from 4 December 2026. The weekly service, marketed by Maersk as G1D, connects ports across southern, southeastern, northeastern and northern Brazil, providing domestic container shipping connections along the country’s coastline. According to DynaLiners, the revised rotation will be: Rio de Janeiro – Itapoá – Santos – Salvador – Suape – Pecém – Manaus – Pecém – Suape – Rio de Janeiro. The service operates with four container vessels, maintaining its weekly frequency. Under the revised arrangement, Aliança will call at Rio Brasil Terminal in the Port of Rio de Janeiro, replacing its existing operations at Sepetiba in Itaguaí. The final scheduled departure from Sepetiba will be performed by Sebastiao Caboto, voyage 648N, on 27 November, while Pedro Alvares Cabral, voyage 649N, will make the first scheduled departure from Rio Brasil Terminal on 4 December. Maersk said the adjustment was intended to support the continuity and reliability of the service, confirming that there would be no changes to vessel deployment, frequency, schedules or operational capacity. The change will maintain the existing domestic cabotage network while shifting the service’s Rio de Janeiro-area port call to a different terminal.

articles.title: Tanker, Passenger Vessel Collide in New Orleans
articles.summary: A tanker ship collided on Friday, November 13, 2026 with an American Cruise Lines passenger ship that was docked in New Orleans on the Mississippi River, where rescue efforts were under way for multiple passengers in the water.US Department…
articles.body: Tanker, Passenger Vessel Collide in New Orleans Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. By Brad Brooks November 13, 2026 American Heritage. Image courtesy American Cruise Line A tanker ship collided on Friday, November 13, 2026 with an American Cruise Lines passenger ship that was docked in New Orleans on the Mississippi River, where rescue efforts were under way for multiple passengers in the water. US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote on social media that "we are throwing every asset we have to helping rescue missing passengers" and that his department was coordinating closely with state officials. The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on details of the missing passengers. The New Orleans mayor's office stated on social media that "multiple individuals have been rescued, and search-and-rescue operations remain ongoing." The US Coast Guard said in an emailed statement that it had responded to the collision and that all river traffic was closed in the vicinity. It provided no other details. Local TV showed videos of the cruise ship listing on its side, while CBS News reported that at least 14 people had been rescued from the water. The cruise ship has a capacity for 150 people and was built in 2015, American Cruise Lines said on its website. The Advocate newspaper, citing unnamed Port of New Orleans officials, reported that 129 passengers were aboard the American Heritage cruise ship when it was hit by the Atlantic Asphalt, a tanker, at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time (1830 GMT). There was no immediate word on any deaths or injuries. The Port of New Orleans did not immediately respond to requests for comment. American Cruise Lines said in an emailed statement that it was coordinating with the US Coast Guard and local authorities. "Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved," the company said. (Reporting by Ismail Shakil, Brad Brooks, Christian Martinez and Ryan Jones; Editing by Edmund Klamann)

articles.body: King Ocean Services has consolidated its two weekly container shipping services between Port Everglades in Florida and Haiti into a single rotation, reducing the number of vessels deployed on the trade from two to one. Under the revised arrangement, Port-au-Prince will retain its weekly connection with Port Everglades, while calls at Cap-Haïtien will be reduced to a fortnightly frequency. The new port rotation will be: Port Everglades – Port-au-Prince – Cap-Haïtien (fortnightly) – Port Everglades. The consolidation represents a reduction in the carrier’s vessel deployment on the Haiti trade, combining the previously separate weekly connections into one service covering both Haitian ports. While Port-au-Prince will continue receiving weekly calls, the revised schedule will halve the frequency of direct calls at Cap-Haïtien, changing the availability of regular shipping connections for cargo moving through the northern Haitian port. The adjustment maintains King Ocean’s coverage of both destinations from South Florida, although with reduced service frequency at Cap-Haïtien. The carrier has not specified the vessel assigned to the consolidated service or the exact implementation date of the revised rotation.

articles.title: Shipping sector backs an International Maritime Organization (IMO) climate deal, but not all of the details
articles.summary: New analysis from the global think tank InfluenceMap confirms, with detailed evidence, broad public support across the shipping and fuels sectors for a climate deal at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). However, differing advocacy positions on key components of the framework, including the carbon price,...
articles.body: Shipping sector backs an International Maritime Organization (IMO) climate deal, but not all of the details in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 14/11/2026 New analysis from the global think tank InfluenceMap confirms, with detailed evidence, broad public support across the shipping and fuels sectors for a climate deal at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). However, differing advocacy positions on key components of the framework, including the carbon price, fuel standard, and rules for counting fuel emissions, threaten to weaken the proposed framework as negotiations resume this month, ahead of MEPC 85 (from 30 November) and the resumed adoption session on 4 December. InfluenceMap identified high-level support for the IMO Net Zero Framework (NZF) from 13 companies and industry associations. Companies and industry associations alike have emphasized the need for a global framework to provide regulatory certainty for the industry’s energy transition, and reaffirmed their support for the IMO as global regulator. The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), which represents over 80% of the world’s merchant fleet, and the World Shipping Council (WSC), which represents 90% of global liner shipping capacity, in 2025 urged governments to adopt the NZF as a “carefully balanced regulatory package”. European Shipowners (ECSA) has called global regulation essential “to deliver the energy transition of international shipping.” Other companies and associations that have shown support include CMA CGM, COSCO Shipping, Hapag-Lloyd, Moller-Maersk, Mediterranean Shipping Company, FuelsEurope, Ipieca, Renewable Fuels Association, Shell, and SEA-LNG. However, in the past year, industry’s support for the Net-Zero Framework has become more cautious. Since adoption was postponed in October 2025, the main shipping associations, including the ICS and WSC, have avoided naming the framework, instead asking governments to “consider all options.” They have not proposed specific changes, but this softer messaging leaves room for a weaker deal. A significant risk remains that the IMO will deliver an agreement that undermines the global shipping industry’s ability to decarbonize, with less ambitious proposals creating a landing zone that moves the IMO away from the net-zero trajectory it agreed to in its 2023 GHG Strategy: net-zero emissions by or around 2050, with cuts of at least 20% by 2030 and 70% by 2040. The NZF has two linked parts, a fuel standard that tightens over time and a carbon price on ships that miss it, both resting on life-cycle rules for counting each fuel’s emissions. InfluenceMap found engagement on these key elements from 4 industry associations: ICS, WSC, Ipieca and SEA-LNG. WSC supported all three elements. ICS broadly supported a carbon price but pushed for a weaker fuel standard ahead of the NZF’s approval in April 2025. Since then, Ipieca and SEA-LNG, representing oil and gas and LNG fuel interests, have advocated against strict GHG life-cycle rules. Carbon Pricing: ICS and WSC both backed a carbon price, but ICS argued for a low and narrow one. Ahead of the NZF’s approval in April 2025, ICS proposed a carbon price of USD 10–20 per tonne of CO2e, charged only on emissions from burning fuel, not from producing it. WSC backed a carbon price set high enough to make clean fuels competitive, illustrated at USD 74 per tonne in 2030. Both organizations have had limited public positioning on the policy since April 2025. Fuel Standard: WSC backed an ambitious standard; ICS argued for a weaker one. In 2024-25, ICS backed a fuel standard but proposed a 30% cut in fuel GHG intensity by 2040, less than half the 65% in the approved NZF. WSC supported the IMO’s fuel standard and its GHG intensity targets. Both organizations have had limited public positioning on the policy since April 2025. SEA-LNG opposed proposals that fuels should meet a minimum GHG threshold to count towards the standard. Accounting Rules: Ipieca and SEA-LNG pushed to lower fossil fuels’ counted emissions; WSC backed stricter accounting. Since April 2025, Ipieca has advocated for replacing the IMO’s cautious default values for fossil fuels with averages and letting certificates stand in for clean power. SEA-LNG argued that LNG’s production emissions are lower than regulators assume. Both would make it easier for LNG-powered ships to comply. The sharpest divide is between sectors. Shipping associations have broadly backed the framework’s core elements. Meanwhile, oil and gas sector groups have publicly supported the NZF while pushing at the IMO for accounting rules that would make fossil fuels, particularly LNG, count as cleaner. These rules decide how strict the framework is in practice, so loosening them could weaken it without changing the headline targets. The accounting rules are on the agenda when the IMO’s working group meets on 23–27 November. Notably, InfluenceMap’s research found that support for the NZF often comes at the expense of regional regulations currently in force. ICS, WSC, SEA-LNG, and European Shipowners (ECSA) have leveraged support for a global framework to advocate against the FuelEU Maritime regulation and the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), calling for the review, harmonization, or withdrawal of these EU-level regulations following the passage of the IMO NZF, despite these rules already being in force and central to meeting EU climate targets. Emily Zhang, Analyst at InfluenceMap, said: “As member states reconvene for MEPC 85, certain governments will invoke corporate interests to justify opposing an ambitious IMO climate deal. This is directly at odds with the industry’s own advocacy. While industry’s top-line support is clear, its ambition for how far GHG regulations should go leaves much to be desired. It is critical that the framework remains grounded in science-based policy and targets already agreed upon at the IMO, rather than being directed by industry preference. The next round of negotiations risks hollowing out a hard-fought multilateral achievement and losing the best opportunity we have to drive the shipping sector’s energy transition.”. Source: InfluenceMap 2026-11-14 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: InfluenceMap identified high-level support for the IMO Net Zero Framework (NZF) from 13 companies and industry associations.
However, in the past year, industry’s support for the Net-Zero Framework has become more cautious.
The NZF has two linked parts, a fuel standard that tightens over time and a carbon price on ships that miss it, both resting on life-cycle rules for counting each fuel’s emissions.

articles.body: Tanker Market Surged in October in Hellenic Shipping News 14/11/2026 D irty tanker spot freight rates surged in October, with record VLCC rates driving Suezmax and Aframax rates higher, OPEC said in its latest monthly report issued this week. The return of disrupted volumes, ongoing trade dislocations, export inefficiencies and longer voyages kept tanker availability constrained. VLCC rates stood at more than ten-times year-ago levels. On the Middle East-to-East route, VLCC spot freight rates rose 26%, m-o-m, in October, while rates on the West Africa-to-East route increased 56%, m-o-m, building on sharply higher gains the month before. Suezmax spot freight rates experienced the largest increase, m-o-m, of the three major vessel classes. On the USGC-to-Europe route, Suezmax rates rose 139%, m-o-m. Compared to the same period last year, spot freight rates were seven times higher. Aframax rates rose further in October, although to a lesser degree than the larger classes. On the Cross-Med route, Aframax spot freight rates gained 67%, m-o-m, more than four times higher compared to year ago levels. The clean tanker market began to see some pressure from the high rates on the crude transport side. On average, clean rates rose 51%, m-o-m, with West of Suez rates catching to the gains seen last month in the East of Suez. Dirty tanker freight rates Very large crude carriers (VLCC) VLCC spot freight rates were the key drive of the tanker market in October, with record high rates pressuring Suezmax, Aframax and even the clean tanker market. On average, VLCC spot freight rates increased 33%, m-o-m, and were up 920%, or more than ten times higher, y-o-y. On the Middle East-to-East route, spot freight rates averaged WS1,213 in October. This represents a m-o-m increase of 26% and more than thirteen times higher than the same month last year. On the Middle East-toWest route, spot freight rates averaged WS550. This represents an increase of 25%, m-o-m, while y-o-y rates were almost ten times higher, y-o-y. Rates on the West Africa-to-East route saw the biggest jump among VLCC routes in October, with an increase of 56% over the previous month to reach WS656. Compared to the previous year, rates were more than seven times higher. Suezmax Suezmax rates experienced the largest increase in October, as record high VLCC rates made switching to smaller vessels economically attractive. On average, Suez spot freight rates increased 132%, m-o-m. Compared with the same month last year, Suezmax rates were about seven times higher. On the West Africa-to-USGC route, spot freight rates averaged WS845 in October, representing an increase of 127%, m-o-m. Compared with year-ago levels, rates were more than seven time higher. Rates on the USGCto-Europe route averaged WS749, reflecting a 139% increase over the previous month. Y-o-y, rates were seven times higher. Aframax Aframax spot freight rates were less pressure than the higher vessel classes. Rates in October were just off record levels seen earlier this year. On average, rates increased 91%, m-o-m. Compared with the same month in 2025, Aframax rates were more than four times higher. Spot freight rates on the Indonesia-to-East route increased by 141%, m-o-m, to average WS740. Y-o-y, rates on the route were five times higher. Rates on the Caribbean-to-US East Coast (USEC) route increased by 94%, m-o-m, to average W808. articles.title: Resistance for shipping’s record rally
articles.summary: Shipping markets are enjoying the strongest and longest earnings boom seen in more than two decades, yet asset buyers remain remarkably cautious about the industry’s longer-term prospects. According to Danish Ship Finance’s November Shipping Market Review, the disconnect between soaring earnings and more restrained...
articles.body: Resistance for shipping’s record rally in International Shipping News 14/11/2026 S hipping markets are enjoying the strongest and longest earnings boom seen in more than two decades, yet asset buyers remain remarkably cautious about the industry’s longer-term prospects. According to Danish Ship Finance’s November Shipping Market Review, the disconnect between soaring earnings and more restrained vessel valuations reflects a widespread belief that current market conditions are temporary rather than structural. The report examines whether investors are right to assume that today’s record profitability will fade. Its conclusion is that while much of the additional shipping demand generated by geopolitical disruption appears durable, but some of the most lucrative sectors, particularly crude tankers, remain highly exposed to a sudden reversal. The current market strength is unprecedented in duration. Yet vessel buyers are not behaving as though the boom will endure. The report argues that market participants are effectively pricing in a short-term earnings spike rather than a prolonged cycle. As the report notes, “buyers are paying for months of record earnings, not years”. The evidence lies in tanker asset values. While tanker earnings have reached record territory, younger and older vessels have appreciated by roughly the same amount. A 15-year-old suezmax has gained about as much value as a newbuild equivalent, suggesting investors are focused on capturing immediate cash flow rather than long-term earning power. According to the report, “had buyers believed the record would last, the young ship, with two more decades of work ahead, would have gained far more”. Longer journeys A central theme of the analysis is that shipping demand has been reshaped less by cargo growth than by longer voyage distances. Since 2019, fleets across every major shipping segment have expanded faster than the underlying cargo volumes they transport. Under normal circumstances, such fleet growth would depress utilisation and freight rates. Instead, vessels remain employed because journeys are taking significantly longer. The report explains that “ships have found work in longer journeys, not more cargo”. Longer round trips, increased ballast voyages, slower sailing speeds, sanctions-related trade shifts and rerouting around geopolitical flashpoints have all absorbed vessel capacity. For LPG carriers, an average round voyage that took 41 days in 2019 now requires 55 days, reducing annual cargo-carrying productivity by roughly a quarter. Danish Ship Finance estimates that roughly one vessel in ten across the major shipping sectors is employed only because round trips have lengthened compared with 2019. These “extra ships” account for all additional LPG carrier employment, most of the increase in bulk carrier demand and around two-thirds of LNG carrier utilisation growth. The report identifies four distinct drivers behind this extra employment: the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea disruptions, Russian sanctions and longer-lasting structural changes in trade patterns. Each carries a different timeline and risk profile. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has had the most immediate impact. Asian buyers have increasingly sourced crude oil and gas cargoes from Atlantic Basin suppliers rather than the Gulf, extending voyage distances considerably. This factor alone is keeping six out of ten extra crude tankers employed and nearly half of the additional LPG carrier capacity in use. Importantly, these ships could return to the market quickly if the waterway reopens. By contrast, Russian sanctions have produced a much more durable shift. Russian energy exports now travel to more distant destinations, while Europe has replaced Russian supplies with imports from other regions. According to the report, this change is keeping six in ten additional product tankers, four in ten extra LNG carriers and three in ten extra crude tankers employed. The authors suggest these patterns would disappear only if sanctions themselves were lifted. Underlying many markets are longer-term structural shifts that appear unlikely to reverse. Growing Asian demand for Atlantic Basin ore, bauxite and gas has permanently altered trade flows, while slower steaming remains widespread. These factors continue to support dry bulk and gas carrier employment. Risk build-up Despite these supportive factors, Danish Ship Finance warns that risk is accumulating in several sectors where four conditions overlap: record earnings, elevated vessel prices, demand support that could disappear quickly and significant fleet growth. Crude tankers are the segment most exposed to a correction. “Crude Tankers are the most exposed; LPG Carriers are adding the most ships,” the report says. If the Strait of Hormuz were to reopen, eight out of every hundred crude tankers could return to the market within weeks while earnings and vessel values remain at historically elevated levels. Compounding the challenge is a substantial orderbook. Although headline industry figures imply that new vessel deliveries merely replace ageing tonnage, the reality varies significantly by segment and vessel class. The report argues that scrapping alone will not be sufficient to offset incoming supply in several key markets. For VLCCs, suezmaxes, capesizes and large gas carriers, the orderbook exceeds the entire fleet of vessels older than 20 years. Even if every eligible ship were scrapped, fleet growth would still happen. The implications for asset values could be severe. Danish Ship Finance calculates that a weaker freight market combined with shorter operating lives could cut the value of older VLCCs dramatically. A ten-year-old VLCC could lose up to 65% of its value under such a scenario, while a 15-year-old unit could lose more than 80%. The report concludes that vessel buyers are largely justified in their cautious stance. Around 1,800 vessels across the five major segments are employed solely because round trips have become longer than they were before 2019. Nearly half of this support appears durable, particularly in dry bulk and sanction-driven trades. However, a substantial share depends on recent geopolitical developments that could change rapidly. “Almost half of the extra work looks set to last,” yet at the same time, “the top layer could go within weeks”, particularly for crude tankers. Freight rates would likely react even before vessels physically return to the market. Source: Baltic Exchange Tops 2026-11-14 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The report examines whether investors are right to assume that today’s record profitability will fade.
The current market strength is unprecedented in duration.
Yet vessel buyers are not behaving as though the boom will endure.

articles.body: IMO may codify alternative net-zero bunker rules in 2027: US FMC in International Shipping News 14/11/2026 The International Maritime Organization (IMO) may start forming consensus around an alternative Net-Zero Framework (NZF) in the coming weeks before hammering out its final text in 2027, US Federal Maritime Commission Chairman Laura DiBella said Nov. 11. The UN agency is due to hold meetings Nov. 23-Dec. 4 to discuss the framework, after member states last year voted to delay its adoption by a year amid fierce US opposition. “I hope we’re going to come to some sort of landing spot,” DiBella told Platts on the sidelines of the International Bunker Industry Association’s annual convention in New York City. “I don’t think anything will be codified this year — maybe 2027, it will be codified. But I think we’ll come to some sort of consensus,” DiBella said. The comments from the top US maritime regulator came after Japan, Panama, and some other countries proposed several alternatives to the NZF, which, in its current form, would place a mandatory cost on maritime greenhouse gas emissions from 2028 to promote a low-carbon bunker transition. The US has estimated that the framework would cost the shipping industry $53 billion-$265 billion annually while arguing the incremental expenses would be ultimately passed on to businesses and consumers. “We have the potential to take remedial action against the flag states that support it, that deliver cargo to the US,” DiBella said, referring to the FMC’s remit. “As the largest consumer of imported goods, we will face the biggest penalties. We don’t need additional inflationary measures on our cargo.” But Washington would be open to what it believes to be a commercially realistic, technology-neutral NZF with achievable emissions targets, voluntary market-based compliance, and no mandatory carbon bills collected by the IMO, the US has suggested. “The United States is working toward a consensus on something so that industry can make the necessary investments [in alternative fuels] and move ahead,” DiBella said. Gas pathway DiBella has displayed a favorable attitude toward LNG and bio-LNG and previously said in a web post that based on her personal view, the fuels could meet over 60% of global maritime bunker demand by 2050, and that the US is well positioned to supply the fuels as the world’s top LNG exporter, which could draw investments in increasing bio-LNG output with a “well-designed global fuel standard. “The infrastructure is there to support it globally … I lean very heavy on the infrastructure side and what’s available and what’s realistic,” she told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. October’s average bunker prices for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil were $17.90/gigajoule in Rotterdam, compared with $28.78/GJ for LNG and $51.71/GJ for bio-LNG, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator. Source: Platts 2026-11-14 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Xeneta Schedule Reliability Scorecard – October 2026: Less than a quarter of global vessels arrive on-time and Gemini’s lead disappears on Asian trades in International Shipping News 14/11/2026 A note on methodology. Figures in this month’s edition use data pulled on 9 November and differ from our Outlook pulled on 26 October. Later October arrivals change some on-time figures by 1-2 percentage points. Global on-time arrivals are now at 24%, a lower reading than the 25% in late October. Far East to Europe also shifted slightly to 7% from 5% on-time, due to an increase in on-time arrivals in the final week of the month. Less than a quarter of global vessels arrive on-time and Gemini’s lead disappears on Asian trades Global on-time arrivals declined for a fifth consecutive month to 24% in October, 3pp below September and now at their lowest monthly average since July 2022. Average delay picked up another 0.4 days, now at +6.4 days across all arrivals. The pace of the fall picked up some speed against the 2pp decline from August to September, and reversing this trend will be an uphill battle. Trades: The Middle East sets a historic low with 12% on-time and Far East to Europe stays near the floor Far East to Europe improved ever so modestly by 3pp up to 7% on-time in October and scaled average delays back to 9.0 days. Far East to North America held flat at 19% on-time and delays eased to 6.3 days. Asia-dependent trades continue to struggle, with minimal gains against low baselines making a recovery above 25% unlikely before 2027. Middle East schedule deterioration reveals progressive wear on alternative Persian Gulf gateways. Down by 2pp to 12%, the trade is now at its lowest on-time since the beginning of this data series in January 2020. As what was initially a temporary network design is retrofitted to permanence, there is still little slack to spare despite improvements to inland corridor transportation and the restriction of merchant haulage volumes in hubs like Jeddah. Europe to North America leads again this month at 53% on-time and just 2.0 days of average delay, a stark contrast to the other E/W arteries and the lowest delays of any global trade. Carriers & Alliances: Gemini falls behind non-alliance services on two major trades The spread between carriers has narrowed yet again, from 42pp down to 36pp, slicing the reputation of its top performers. Maersk lost 7pp to 39% in October, the largest fall of any carrier, while Hapag-Lloyd held at 41% on-time. Wan Hai and Yang Ming, at 5% and 6% respectively, have been in the bottom three for five months running. Gemini’s on-time lead over non-alliance services has declined sharply since September. Split by trade, it has disappeared entirely on both Far East to Europe (7% vs 23%) and Far East to North America (18% vs 39%), where their services now run 16pp and 21pp below non-alliance strings. On Far East to Europe, Gemini’s average delay is 9.4 days; longer than Ocean Alliance (6.8 days) and MSC (7.8 days) but still short of non-alliance services (9.9 days) and Premier Alliance (11.0 days). Carriers charging a premium for reliability will have to defend their positions trade-by-trade this tender season. Shippers should ask for lane-level reliability as a progressive time series, not alliance averages or 6-month trade values, before agreeing to 2027 contract rates. Port Congestion: Africa leads and Shanghai’s queue unravels without yielding trade recovery Africa still leads the regional congestion rankings, with 33% of vessels waiting on any given day and 2.8 days of average wait. The port of Beira alone averages 12.8 days of wait and a 79% waiting ratio – those numbers are not skewed by any single hull. The Middle East follows at 1.9 days and a 27% queue, with 81% of vessels waiting at Fujairah and 64% at Khor Fakkan in the Gulf of Oman, against 17% at Jeddah in the Red Sea. Northeast Asia saw the wait share ease from 30% to 26%, but the underlying problem is stubborn: chronically embedded schedule delays rarely unravel at the same pace as vessel queues. Shanghai’s average daily queue fell from 86 to 36 vessels in October, but carriers still omitted 35% of scheduled loading calls at the hub on Far East to North America services, compared to 0% in October 2025. Spotlight Blanks picked up in October on all three East-West trades but only transatlantic increased against 2025 As expected with the windfall of Chinese Golden Week and the Autumn Festival, carriers blanked 18% of planned capacity on Far East to Europe, up from 6% in September, but still below 21% of planned TEU in October 2025. Part of that gap is explained by schedules; planned capacity also grew 15% year-on-year so blanked TEU in the month of October is roughly level at 407,000 TEU in 2025 vs 396,000 TEU in 2026. On Far East to North America, carriers removed 14% of planned capacity, up from 7% in September, and a 4pp drop against October 2025. Planned TEU has grown by just 4% against last year, so the drop was genuinely less blanking on this trade, from 467,000 TEU in October 2025 to 393,000 TEU in 2026. These blanks supported the reliability lift by the same small margin in both years. In October 2025, the 21% blanked on Far East to Europe propped a 3pp rise from 22% to 25% in on-time arrivals. This October, an 18% blanked rate nudged on-time another 3pp from 4% to 7%. Built on a baseline 18pp lower than 2025; the delays in the network are too deep for cancelled sailings to reset reliability in a meaningful measure. What to watch • Tenders are being set against a market with little slack to absorb disruptions. With a narrower 36pp on-time band across carriers, the tightest since March 2026, shippers need to book service-level reliability and work on-time, average delay, and cancellation rates into their RFQs. • Don’t take performance for granted, even on steadier lanes. Gemini’s Atlantic lane has weakened from 76-92% on-time every week from late July to 52% in the final week of October. Delay provided an earlier signal: rising from 0.3 days in late September to 1.0 day at the end of October, and again to 1.25 days in early November. • Treat the minimal improvement on Far East to Europe as provisional. An easing in vessel congestion does not mean that a port is freed from berth schedule delays or high yard utilization. The compound effects of back-to-back terminal closures unwind slowly long after vessels start to move. Source: Xeneta Tops 2026-11-14 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Making underwater radiated noise measurement practical for the world fleet
articles.summary: Along with ICS, IPTA and RINA, we have co-sponsored a proposal to MEPC 85 aimed at making underwater radiated noise (URN) measurement practical and affordable for the world fleet. The IMO’s Revised Guidelines (MEPC.1/Circ.906/Rev.1) prefer direct measurement to establish a ship’s URN baseline, and class society quiet...
articles.body: Making underwater radiated noise measurement practical for the world fleet in International Shipping News 14/11/2026 Along with ICS, IPTA and RINA, we have co-sponsored a proposal to MEPC 85 aimed at making underwater radiated noise (URN) measurement practical and affordable for the world fleet. The IMO’s Revised Guidelines (MEPC.1/Circ.906/Rev.1) prefer direct measurement to establish a ship’s URN baseline, and class society quiet ship notations normally require it. The problem Dedicated sea trials cost an estimated USD 30,000–50,000 directly, and USD 40,000–250,000 per ship once diversion and lost revenue are included. Across a fleet of around 100,000 ships, one round of measurements could cost USD 4–25 billion, and repeat measurements may be needed. Yet global capacity is only around 50 dedicated trials a year. The proposed approach • A network of autonomous measurement facilities at major pinch points (for example Suez, Panama, Gibraltar, Malacca, the Taiwan Strait and the English Channel) would measure ships during normal operation • An illustrative network of five facilities would cost roughly USD 0.8–1.8 million in capital and USD 0.7–1.4 million a year to run: under USD 20 per ship in capital and under USD 15 per ship per year in operating costs. Ship-specific data checking and reporting would add around USD 4,424 per ship • An ISO “Measurement of Opportunity” standard is needed for consistent results. It must be rigorous enough for quiet ship notations and repeatable enough to show trends. A network could be established in about four years • Autonomous facilities will not cover everyone (short-sea ships, for example) and are one part of the solution. Onboard measurement, drone-deployed sensors and predictive modelling remain relevant. Why it matters Earlier case studies found that measurement costs below USD 15,500 could make environmental incentive schemes (such as ESI, Green Marine, Green Award, PIAQUO and ECHO) financially beneficial. Affordable baselines would also let shipowners show whether noise-reduction measures actually work. Next steps The co-sponsors are asking the IMO to recognise the importance of economically viable, accessible baseline measurements. They invite further proposals on feasible approaches, and ask that any URN Working Group’s terms of reference cover practical, affordable baselining options and timelines. Source: BIMCO, https://www.bimco.org/news-insights/bimco-news/2026/11/12-imo-urn/ 2026-11-14 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: GMS Week 46 – FREIGHT TAKES THE HELM
articles.summary: Another week has passed without a meaningful change in global ship recycling conditions, although the trading market has strengthened its position once again. articles.body: GMS Week 46 – FREIGHT TAKES THE HELM in Weekly Demolition Reports 14/11/2026 Another week has passed without a meaningful change in global ship recycling conditions, although the trading market has strengthened its position once again. Dry freight has continued its recovery, crude oil has softened further and regional steel prices have offered some encouragement. Recycling indications remain unchanged across all four destinations, with healthy buying interest still frustrated by the persistent shortage of available candidates. Owners continue to enjoy worthwhile trading alternatives, leaving recyclers with limited opportunities to convert their appetite into fresh business. Dry freight provided the week’s clearest movement. The Baltic Dry Index advanced to 3,020 on Thursday, November 12, from 2,740 a week earlier, extending its recovery to seven consecutive sessions. Capesizes strengthened to 4,836, Panamaxes reached 2,117 and Supramaxes improved to 1,831. The broad-based improvement has reinforced employment prospects for ageing bulk carriers, reducing the immediate incentive for owners to consider recycling. For buyers awaiting a sustained freight correction, the market has once again moved in the opposite direction. Oil prices continued to retreat, with Brent trading around USD 95.50 per barrel on Friday and WTI near USD 88. Expectations of reduced military escalation in the Middle East have weighed on crude, although continuing attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure demonstrate that regional security risks remain unresolved. Lower energy costs may offer some relief to recycling operations and steel production, but uncertain trading conditions continue to influence tanker employment and owners’ disposal decisions. Steel markets offered a somewhat firmer picture. Bangladesh plate strengthened during the week, while Pakistan recovered modestly from its recent correction. Indian steel also improved towards Friday, although Chinese quotations remained unchanged. These movements provide some welcome support to recycler margins without creating a compelling case for higher vessel bids. Currency conditions remain particularly important in Bangladesh, where Dollar appreciation continues to complicate purchasing calculations despite central bank intervention. Physical waterfront activity also continued, although fresh transactions remain limited. Chattogram recorded further deliveries and smaller vessel arrivals, while Alang received another chemical tanker and updated the delivery status of previously arrived tonnage. Gadani reported no new movements. These developments reflect the progression of earlier purchases rather than a significant replenishment of the recycling sales pipeline. Bangladesh continues to lead conventional buying sentiment, supported by improving seasonal conditions and stronger local steel. India retains its specialist advantages despite regulatory uncertainty, while Pakistan remains competitive but measured. Turkey continues to operate selectively amid mixed steel-market developments, including disruption at a major domestic mill. The overall market remains stable, with no major change in its underlying commercial direction. Buyers are maintaining their positions, but stronger freight has once again demonstrated why owners remain reluctant to release ageing vessels. Steel may be providing some encouragement, yet profitable trading continues to offer a more persuasive alternative. For now, the beaches have the interest and the capacity. The trading market still has the upper hand. For Week 46 of 2026, GMS Market Rankings / Vessel indications are as below. articles.body: DP World is accelerating development of two ports in Fujairah, investments of around AED 2.5 billion, as the UAE strengthens alternative shipping routes to keep goods moving despite disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Phased operations are now expected to begin within 18 to 24 months, compared with an earlier estimate of 24 to 30 months. Under a 50-year concession, the company will develop the Al Rugaylat container and multipurpose terminal and the Dibba General Cargo terminal. Al Rugaylat, near Fujairah International Airport, will have capacity of about 2.5 million TEUs a year, 1.7 million tonnes of general cargo and 190,000 car equivalent units, and will accommodate the latest generation of ultra-large container ships. Dibba will add up to 3.6 million tonnes of general cargo capacity a year for conventional freight and vehicles. Together they will lift DP World’s UAE container capacity from 19.4 million TEUs to almost 22 million TEUs, and both will connect to Jebel Ali and the Jebel Ali Free Zone through the company’s inland logistics network. The aim is a long-term network in which cargo can enter through the port best suited to its destination, whether or not Hormuz shipping is fully restored. Between early March and the end of October, DP World moved more than one million TEUs by truck and rail from east coast ports to Jebel Ali and domestic markets. Cargo enters through ports outside the Strait before travelling overland to Dubai for customs clearance, storage and distribution. Shehab Mohamad Aljasmi, Chief Commercial Officer for Ports and Terminals at DP World GCC, said Jebel Ali stayed open throughout, with operations limited for just six hours since the crisis began. The company built a trucking network of more than 3,000 vehicles, 700 of them its own, and about 3,500 TEUs a day now move through land corridors supported by links via Sohar and Duqm in Oman and Jeddah in Saudi Arabia. It also opened the Jebel Ali Rail Terminal and a 100,000 square metre empty-container depot at Al Awir. Dubai Customs and Oman Customs activated a Green Corridor within 72 hours, letting sealed trucks carry containers directly to Jebel Ali under customs control, facilitating trade worth around AED 34 billion between 1 March and 30 June. DP World expects shipping services and volumes at Jebel Ali, which has 19.4 million TEUs of annual capacity, over 80 weekly services and handled 15.6 million TEUs in 2025, to recover within one to three months once safe passage is restored. Meetings with nine shipping lines in Asia showed interest in returning, with the pace depending on how quickly operators reposition vessels and reorganise networks. The Jebel Ali Free Zone, home to more than 12,000 companies across about 57 square kilometres, attracted over AED 1 billion in new investment in the first half of 2026, with occupancy above 90% overall, 94% for land and 99 percent for warehouses, and office occupancy at a ten-year high. The South Container Terminal at Jeddah Islamic Port set cargo records in July and October after expansion to four million TEUs of annual capacity, and the US$ 250 million Jeddah Logistics Park is due to open in the first quarter of 2027. Development continues at the Al Rawdah Special Economic Zone near the Oman-UAE border, and no major regional investment has been suspended. Going forward, DP World is prioritising permanent cross-border transport connections, faster customs information exchange and pre-agreed procedures so that alternative routes can be activated more quickly in future disruptions, a longer-term shift toward multiple routes for the UAE’s imports and exports rather than reliance on a single maritime gateway.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo credit: Tow Boaters Facebook group Update: ‘Miracle on the Mississippi’: All Accounted For After Tanker Capsizes Cruise Ship in New Orleans A Marshall Islands-flagged asphalt tanker struck the docked American Cruise Lines riverboat American Heritage on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, sending people into the water and leaving the cruise ship capsized at the dock. The 160-meter tanker Atlantic Asphalt collided with the U.S.-flagged American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m. local time below the Crescent City Connection bridge, according to the Port of New Orleans. Video of the incident shows the tanker striking the port side of the docked river cruise ship. In the aftermath, the American Heritage took on water, rolled over and subsequently capsized alongside the dock. Other video circulating online showed people in the water wearing life jackets as rescuers responded. Port NOLA said about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, were aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision. The mayor’s office said multiple people had been rescued and search-and-rescue operations were ongoing. American Cruise Lines confirmed that the American Heritage was involved in a collision while it was docked in New Orleans. “We are in close coordination with the U.S. Coast Guard and local authorities. Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved. We will share more information as it becomes available,” the company said. The collision triggered a major emergency response involving the U.S. Coast Guard, New Orleans Fire Department, police, EMS and Port NOLA Harbor Police. The Coast Guard has closed the river to all vessel traffic between mile marker 93 and 96 while responders assess the situation and conduct response operations. The NTSB is launching a “go team” to investigate the collision. The team expects to arrive tomorrow morning. According to vessel-tracking data from MarineTraffic, the 81-meter American Heritage had arrived from Natchez, Mississippi and docked in New Orleans earlier on Friday. MarineTraffic recorded a “proximity event” involving the Atlantic Asphalt at 18:29 UTC, or 12:29 p.m. local time, corresponding with the reported time of the collision. AIS data shows the Atlantic Asphalt called at Amuay, Venezuela, in mid-October before arriving in Paulsboro, New Jersey, on October 24. The tanker departed Paulsboro on October 26 and arrived in New Orleans on November 11, two days before the collision. The Atlantic Asphalt was not operating under the current Jones Act waiver, as it was continuing an international voyage after discharging part of its foreign-loaded cargo in New Jersey rather than transporting cargo loaded at Paulsboro to New Orleans. The Trump administration’s emergency Jones Act waiver, which was extended Friday, allows certain foreign-flagged vessels to transport domestic cargo between U.S. ports. American Cruise Lines said guests and crew had been evacuated and that it was coordinating with the Coast Guard and local authorities. Passengers were being taken to the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for assistance and medical evaluation. The cause of the collision remains under investigation. Authorities have not said whether the tanker experienced a mechanical or propulsion failure before the impact. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said he had been briefed on the incident and was in contact with local officials as the emergency response continued. The American Heritage, built in 2015, is a 150-passenger paddlewheel river cruise ship operated by American Cruise Lines. The vessel features multiple passenger decks, private balcony accommodations and a traditional stern paddlewheel design. It operates cruises along the Mississippi River and other U.S. inland waterways. This is a developing story and will be updated. articles.body: Services Top Right Tropical Shipping adds St. Croix to Canada Express service November 13, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Tropical Shipping has expanded its Canada Express container service with the addition of St. Croix in the US Virgin Islands, extending the route’s coverage between Canada, Florida and the Caribbean. According to DynaLiners, the revised service is operated by two container vessels, each with a capacity of approximately 1,100 TEU, connecting Halifax with Palm Beach and several Caribbean destinations. The updated port rotation will be: Halifax – Palm Beach – San Juan – St. Thomas – St. Maarten – St. Croix – Halifax. The addition of St. Croix provides another port connection within the Canada Express network, alongside the existing calls in Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands and St. Maarten. Tropical Shipping already maintains operations in St. Croix through its wider Caribbean shipping network. The latest adjustment therefore extends the island’s coverage within the Canada Express service rather than establishing an entirely new destination for the carrier. The revised rotation retains Halifax as its Canadian gateway and Palm Beach as its Florida call, while expanding the service’s Caribbean port coverage to four destinations. articles.body: Nikkiso Delivers Dry Dock Overhaul for LNG Tanker Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 © Nikkiso CE&IG Nikkiso Clean Energy & Industrial Gases Group (Nikkiso CE&IG) has successfully completed a dry-dock maintenance project for the LNG tanker Ekaputra 1, carrying out the overhaul of seven cryogenic pumps in only 10 days. The work was performed for vessel owner Humolco by Nikkiso CE&IG’s Cryogenic Services Business Unit during the tanker’s scheduled dry dock window at PaxOcean shipyard in Batam, Indonesia. The scope included the overhaul of five large cargo pumps and two spray pumps, which all form part of the vessel’s LNG cargo handling operations. Completing seven pump overhauls within a 10-day dry-dock window required careful planning and coordination among Nikkiso CE&IG’s Cryogenic Services team, specialized subcontractors and the shipyard. Nikkiso coordinated personnel, parts and other resources in advance to keep the project on schedule, with all seven pumps overhauled, reinstalled, and recommissioned.

articles.title: Port of Hamburg records slight decline
articles.summary: The Port of Hamburg steadied its cargo handling in the third quarter of 2026, partially offsetting the declines of the first half. articles.body: The Port of Hamburg steadied its cargo handling in the third quarter of 2026, partially offsetting the declines of the first half. Total throughput at Germany’s largest seaport reached 84.5 million tonnes in the first nine months, 2.6% below the same period last year. The shortfall stems mainly from weather-related losses at the start of the year, disruption in the global oil market following the war in Iran and, most recently, strikes. Extensive modernisation work at the container terminals also weighed on results, but it is expected to strengthen the port’s performance and competitiveness and lay the foundations for future growth. Container throughput improved markedly in the third quarter compared with the end of the first half. Over the nine months the port handled 6.1 million TEU, down 2.8% in TEU and 2.6% in tonnes. TEU volumes rose with Singapore (+9.3%), India (+7.8%), Finland (+15.7%) and Sri Lanka (+3.7%). Persistent trade barriers continue to hamper trade with the USA (-9.8%), while volume with China, the port’s largest trading partner, is almost back at last year’s level (-0.6%). Many of the declines visible at the end of the second quarter were partly recovered during the third. Bulk cargo totalled 23.9 million tonnes, down 2.6%. Dry bulk continued to grow, up 1.7% on a significant recovery in grain exports and ore imports, partially offsetting a 13.3% fall in liquid bulk. In other general cargo and vehicles, a positive third quarter reversed the earlier downward trend, with the segment now up 2% at a total of 853 thousand tonnes.

articles.body: Neptune Pacific has brought forward the deployment of ICS Silver Lining on its MICROPAC service and the redeployment of Southern Pearl to its INTRAPAC service, introducing additional cargo capacity across both Central Pacific trades ahead of the peak season. Under the revised arrangements, Southern Pearl will join the INTRAPAC service as voyage 2611, calling at Funafuti, Apia and Wallis and Futuna. The vessel is scheduled to arrive in Funafuti on 19 November, Apia on 24 November, Wallis on 25 November and Futuna on 30 November. Cargo exported from Lautoka to Wallis and Futuna, currently carried aboard Capitaine Wallis voyage 2611, will be transferred to Southern Pearl in Apia. Meanwhile, ICS Silver Lining will enter the MICROPAC service as voyage 2609, loading cargo in Suva before proceeding to Tarawa, Majuro and Christmas Island (Kiritimati). The vessel is scheduled to call at Suva on 21 November, Tarawa on 27 November, Majuro on 3 December and Kiritimati on 12 December. Lautoka export cargo currently aboard Southern Pearl voyage 2609 will be transferred to ICS Silver Lining in Suva. Following the transitional voyages, Southern Pearl will resume the regular INTRAPAC rotation from voyage 2612, while ICS Silver Lining will return to the standard MICROPAC rotation from voyage 2610. The carrier said the accelerated deployments would provide additional cargo capacity to accommodate peak season demand across both services. Neptune Pacific also acknowledged that the revised arrangements would result in cargo disruptions and advised affected customers to contact its customer service team or local representatives for assistance.

Join the leading maritime news network FILE PHOTO: Oil/Chemical Tanker "Bald Man" at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo Global oil markets are beginning to recover from the Iran war, but shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted, with vessel traffic roughly 65% below pre-conflict levels and tanker attacks continuing across the region. Separate reports released Friday by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) highlight the uneven recovery in energy trade nearly nine months after the conflict began. The IEA said global oil supplies are on track to exceed demand by 1.7 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, reversing its previous forecast of a deficit as Persian Gulf producers restore disrupted exports. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, climbed to 18.4 million barrels per day in October, just 26% below pre-war levels. Crude shipments accounted for much of the recovery, reaching 15 million barrels per day, or about 82% of pre-war volumes. Yet the rebound in oil shipments has not translated into a broader recovery in vessel traffic. Hormuz Traffic Remains Deeply Disrupted In its latest weekly assessment, UKMTO reported 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits through the Strait of Hormuz, with overall traffic still approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. The figures combine AIS-tracked vessel movements with U.S.-reported facilitated transits, including ships operating without broadcasting AIS signals. UKMTO cautioned that it could not independently verify the U.S. figures. The security situation remains dangerous. UKMTO documented eight maritime security incidents during its latest reporting period, including seven tanker attacks. Five incidents occurred in the Strait of Hormuz, two in the Arabian Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. Three vessels continued their voyages, three required assistance and the outcomes of two remained unknown. None was reported sunk. UKMTO also noted that while most AIS-broadcasting vessels continue to use the Iranian route, more ships are using the southern passage. Most reported projectile strikes since July 6 have occurred along that southern route. More Oil Moving, But Shipping Costs Remain High The recovery in Gulf exports is beginning to ease pressure on global oil markets. According to the IEA, observed oil inventories increased by 52 million barrels in October, while oil volumes on the water jumped by 86 million barrels to their highest level since January. For tanker operators, however, conditions remain difficult. Freight rates for crude shipments from the Middle East to Asia remain near record levels, according to the IEA, even as rates for Aframax and Suezmax tankers have eased. The contrast underscores the uneven recovery. While Gulf producers have restored substantial crude export volumes, commercial shipping continues to operate under significant security constraints. The IEA’s October export figures and UKMTO’s November vessel counts measure different periods and activity, but together point to a market recovering faster than normal shipping conditions. The improvement has also been concentrated in crude oil. Gulf exports of refined products and liquefied petroleum gas remain at roughly half their pre-war levels, contributing to persistent shortages. Diesel is particularly tight, with European prices still near $180 per barrel, roughly 77% above pre-war levels. To ease the shortage, IEA member countries plan to make another 71 million barrels of emergency stocks available by the end of February, including 15 million barrels of diesel. Meanwhile, the recovery in oil supplies has helped push crude prices sharply lower. North Sea Dated crude has fallen from an October peak of $136 per barrel to around $93, although prices remain well above pre-war levels. The latest reports suggest global oil supplies are recovering despite continued disruption to one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints. But with tanker attacks continuing, freight rates elevated and Hormuz traffic still far below normal, the recovery remains vulnerable to renewed disruption. articles.title: CMA CGM Demonstrates Relative Resilience in a Volatile Q3
articles.summary: The third quarter of 2026 took place in a volatile economic environment, with persistent tensions in the Middle East impacting international trade and global supply chains. In this context, both shipping and logistics activities were affected…
articles.body: CMA CGM Demonstrates Relative Resilience in a Volatile Q3 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 © Michael Derrer Fuchs - stock.adobe.com The third quarter of 2026 took place in a volatile economic environment, with persistent tensions in the Middle East impacting international trade and global supply chains. In this context, both shipping and logistics activities were affected by adjustments made to trade routes and transport networks. Nevertheless, the global economy demonstrated relative resilience given the scale of the shock to energy prices, while international trade remained dynamic. The Group’s transported volumes increased by 5.5% compared with the third quarter of 2025, outperforming the market. This represents one of the strongest growth rates recorded in recent years. This growth was underpinned by three key drivers: Restocking , as companies sought to build up inventories amid ongoing economic and geopolitical uncertainty; Increased investment in AI-related infrastructure and data centres; Strong momentum in clean technologies and electric vehicles , particularly in China, amid higher hydrocarbon prices. The CMA CGM Group leveraged the complementary strengths of its shipping, logistics and terminal operations to offer customers integrated solutions across the entire supply chain. This strategy is underpinned by investments in port infrastructure, which are essential to expanding the Group’s capacity and strengthening its global network. The Group also accelerated its transformation through innovation and artificial intelligence across all its businesses. MAIA, its agentic AI platform co-developed with Mistral AI, is being progressively rolled out to employees across its shipping, logistics and media businesses. In France, the CMA CGM Group confirms its long-term commitment and contribution to the country's economic, maritime and logistics development. The Group supports 96,500 jobs, including 19,100 direct jobs and 77,400 jobs across the wider economy. The Group has welcomed the first vessels in its new series of 24,000-TEU containerships, including the CMA CGM NOTRE DAME, CMA CGM PANTHEON and CMA CGM ORSAY, which are deployed on its flagship FAL service connecting Asia and Europe. These are the world's largest LNG-powered containerships operating under the French flag. CMA CGM also accelerated the energy transition in shipping through several major alternative fuel bunkering operations: bioethanol in Brazil, bio-LNG in Rotterdam and a world-record biomethanol bunkering operation in Shanghai. CEVA Logistics expanded its international footprint through the acquisition of FedEx Supply Chain and initiated a simplification of its organizational structure under the leadership of Patrick Moebel, aimed at improving its efficiency and strengthening customer proximity CMA CGM further developed its global terminal network, notably through Terminal 4 at the Port of Jeddah in partnership with Red Sea Gateway Terminal, and CMA Terminals' acquisition of a 49% stake in Nador Container Terminal in Morocco. CMA CGM AIR CARGO strengthened its operations during the quarter, with a fleet of eight aircraft now operating under the CMA CGM AIR CARGO and Air Belgium brands, supported by hubs in France, Belgium and the United States. CMA Media launched CMA Sport, while BFMTV maintained its position as France's leading news channel throughout the quarter. Outlook Demand for maritime transport benefited from a strong increase in volumes carried, a trend that is expected to continue over the coming months. Freight rates, which have been rising since the second quarter of 2026, are also supporting the growth of the business. However, the outlook for the coming months remains uncertain. Tensions in the Middle East continue to disrupt shipping routes and weigh on operating costs, while changes in trade policies will continue to influence international trade flows. Against this backdrop, the CMA CGM Group maintains a prudent and responsive approach to management. Its presence across the entire logistics chain, the flexibility of its network and the strength of its balance sheet are major assets in order to cope with changes in its operating environment and provide long-term support to its customers.

articles.summary: The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping.

REUTERS/Mohammed Aty LONDON, Nov 13 – The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release of oil from its members’ emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, the Paris-based agency, which advises industrialized countries, said in a monthly report, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. “The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the agency said in the report. Oil prices reversed earlier gains after the IEA report was released at 0900 GMT. Brent crude LCOc1 was last down 0.1% at $95.71 a barrel. The report follows signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports disrupted since the start of the war in late February by using workarounds such as so-called dark crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade attack. The OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia, pumped 41.23 million bpd of crude in October, OPEC said on Wednesday, up about 2.04 million bpd from September and 97% of the pre-war February volume. OTHER ANALYSTS SEE SIGNS OF SURPLUS Other analysts have also forecast a return to excess supply, despite the lack of a resolution to the Iran war and continuing tanker attacks in the Gulf. JPMorgan last week forecast a global surplus of 1.4 million bpd in October. High oil prices have also curbed demand this year, helping tip the balance into a surplus. World oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.7 million bpd in 2026 to 102.3 million bpd before rebounding by 2 million bpd in 2027, the IEA said, little changed from its previous forecasts. As well as rising output from OPEC+, the IEA flagged supply rising from outside the group. Production from the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana will rise by 1.6 million bpd this year, the IEA said. In 2027, global supply is projected to rise by 6.6 million bpd to 108.1 million bpd, led by a further recovery in Gulf output. Still, the 2027 supply growth forecast is down 1.1 million bpd from last month’s report, and the lower outlook partly reflects a downward revision from Iran, the IEA said. Iran is subject to a US blockade that has curbed its oil exports. For 2027, the IEA sees the supply surplus at about 3.8 million bpd, slightly down from a 3.94 million bpd surplus last month. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy CMA CGM French shipping giant CMA CGM more than tripled its third-quarter net profit as higher container freight rates and strong cargo volumes boosted earnings amid ongoing disruptions to global shipping routes in the Middle East. The Marseille-based group reported Friday that net income attributable to the group climbed to $2.32 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up from $760 million a year earlier, an increase of approximately 205%. Revenue rose 31.1% to $18.4 billion, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) jumped 61.6% to $4.78 billion. The group’s EBITDA margin improved to 25.9%, compared with 21% in the same period last year. The strong results were driven primarily by CMA CGM’s container shipping business, which benefited from sustained demand and elevated freight rates as Middle East tensions continued to disrupt maritime trade routes and global supply chains. CMA CGM carried 6.5 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) during the quarter, up 5.5% year-over-year, outperforming the broader market. Shipping revenue surged 37.3% to $12.3 billion, supported by a 30% increase in average revenue per container to $1,891 per TEU. The division generated $4 billion in EBITDA, compared with $2.2 billion a year earlier, lifting its EBITDA margin to 32.4%. The figures underscore how ongoing disruptions in the Middle East are reshaping the container shipping market, supporting freight rates even as carriers face longer voyages, higher operating costs and changes to established trade routes. “In an uncertain geopolitical environment, the Group has delivered a strong performance in the third quarter,” said Rodolphe Saadé, chairman and CEO of CMA CGM. Saadé pointed to growing shipping volumes, positive results from the company’s terminals business and expansion across air freight and logistics as evidence of the group’s ability to adapt to changing market conditions. CMA CGM said global trade remained resilient despite the geopolitical uncertainty and higher energy prices. The company attributed demand growth partly to businesses rebuilding inventories, increased investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centers, and strong demand for clean technologies and electric vehicles, particularly in China. Outside container shipping, the group’s logistics business reported revenue of $5.46 billion, up 19.2% from a year earlier. However, EBITDA declined 14.4% to $366 million, reflecting difficult conditions in freight forwarding and continued weakness in the automotive sector. The company also continued investing in its fleet and global port infrastructure. During the quarter, CMA CGM welcomed the first ships in a new series of 24,000-TEU LNG-powered containerships, including the CMA CGM NOTRE DAME , CMA CGM PANTHEON and CMA CGM ORSAY . The vessels are deployed on the company’s flagship Asia-Europe FAL service and rank among the world’s largest LNG-powered containerships. CMA CGM also expanded its terminal network through a partnership involving Terminal 4 at Saudi Arabia’s Port of Jeddah and the acquisition of a 49% stake in Morocco’s Nador Container Terminal. Looking ahead, CMA CGM expects strong container shipping demand to continue over the coming months , with freight rates that have been rising since the second quarter supporting the business. However, the company warned that the outlook remains uncertain as geopolitical tensions, changing trade policies and disruptions to shipping routes continue to affect global cargo flows. “Tensions in the Middle East continue to disrupt shipping routes and weigh on operating costs,” CMA CGM said in its outlook. The company said its diversified operations, flexible shipping network and strong balance sheet would help it navigate the uncertain trading environment. articles.summary: German container shipping giant Hapag-Lloyd reported a sharp increase in third-quarter earnings as higher freight rates more than offset rising operating costs tied to the Middle East conflict and widespread...
