Join the leading maritime news network A hapag-lloyd ship at dock German container shipping giant Hapag-Lloyd reported a sharp increase in third-quarter earnings as higher freight rates more than offset rising operating costs tied to the Middle East conflict and widespread port congestion. The Hamburg-based carrier reported Thursday that third-quarter net profit jumped to $999 million, up from $172 million a year earlier, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) nearly doubled to $1.73 billion. Revenue climbed 26% to $6.88 billion, driven largely by stronger freight rates and high vessel utilization across its global container network. The company’s average freight rate increased 28% to $1,808 per twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU), compared with $1,413 in the third quarter of 2025. Transport volumes remained essentially flat at 3.38 million TEU, reflecting continued operational disruptions and capacity constraints. Hapag-Lloyd said the Middle East conflict and congestion at major ports continued to push up operating costs, but higher rates and efficiency improvements more than offset those pressures. “We delivered a strong third quarter, driven by significantly higher spot rates, robust demand and high capacity utilization,” said CEO Rolf Habben Jansen. Operating profit (EBIT) surged to $1.09 billion from $228 million a year earlier. The strong results prompted Hapag-Lloyd to raise its full-year earnings guidance for the third time this year. The company now expects EBITDA of $4.6 billion to $5.0 billion, up from its previous forecast of $3.9 billion to $4.4 billion. Its operating profit forecast was also raised to between $2.0 billion and $2.4 billion, compared with an earlier range of $1.25 billion to $1.75 billion. Red Sea Services Gradually Return The earnings announcement comes as Hapag-Lloyd and its Gemini Cooperation partner Maersk continue gradually restoring container services through the Red Sea and Suez Canal after extended diversions around Africa. In its third-quarter investor presentation , Hapag-Lloyd highlighted the phased return to the shorter Suez route, which it said would reduce transit times, improve Mediterranean connectivity and strengthen schedule reliability. The carrier identified several Asia-Europe services now routed through Suez, including five Far East–South Europe services, one Far East–North Europe service and two India–Europe connections. Other northern European services continue to use the Cape of Good Hope route. Earlier this month, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd announced that their joint ME1 India–Europe service, known as IOS at Hapag-Lloyd, would switch from the Cape of Good Hope to the Suez Canal. The first westbound departure was scheduled from Salalah on November 4, with the first eastbound departure from Tangier scheduled for November 12–13. The partners have emphasized that further routing decisions remain dependent on security conditions in the Red Sea. The return to Suez could have broader implications for global container shipping capacity. Shorter voyages reduce the number of vessels needed to maintain regular services, potentially releasing capacity that had been tied up in longer diversions around southern Africa. For now, however, Hapag-Lloyd continues to benefit from tight capacity and elevated freight rates. Terminals Business Expands Hapag-Lloyd’s terminal operations also contributed to the improved results. Revenue from its Terminal & Infrastructure segment rose to $197 million from $131 million a year earlier, supported by investments in terminal capacity and improved performance in Latin America and India. The segment’s EBITDA increased to $56 million from $30 million. Despite the strong third quarter, Hapag-Lloyd’s net profit for the first nine months of 2026 was $827 million, down from $946 million in the same period last year, reflecting weaker profitability earlier in the year. The carrier said fourth-quarter performance was developing better than previously expected, supported by continued strong spot freight rates. Still, Hapag-Lloyd cautioned that freight-rate volatility and persistent geopolitical risks leave considerable uncertainty surrounding its full-year outlook. (File photo: Ken Lund/Wikimedia Commons) A Singapore-flagged bulk carrier struck the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge on the Delaware River Thursday afternoon, leaving the movable span temporarily unable to close and prompting a U.S. Coast Guard inspection of the vessel. The incident occurred around 1:15 p.m. as the 591-foot (180-meter) Strategic Alliance was transiting the river with the bridge’s draw span open for marine traffic, according to the Coast Guard. The vessel, identified in shipping databases as a roughly 40,000-dwt bulk carrier (IMO 9648075), was subsequently moored at a Kinder Morgan facility in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where Coast Guard inspectors were dispatched to assess its condition. No injuries were reported. The circumstances of the collision remain unclear, including which part of the bridge the vessel struck and whether the ship sustained any damage. Authorities have not disclosed what cargo the vessel was carrying or identified a cause for the incident. The bridge, which connects Philadelphia with Palmyra, New Jersey, initially remained in the raised position following the strike. Pennsylvania state Rep. Ed Neilson reported that the bridge was unable to close, triggering major traffic disruptions on both sides of the Delaware River. According to the Associated Press , the Coast Guard said the bridge also remained open to allow another vessel to pass through before the span was eventually lowered. The Burlington County Bridge Commission, which operates the crossing, began inspecting the structure and assessing the extent of the damage. The Tacony-Palmyra Bridge, opened in 1929, spans a navigable section of the Delaware River used by commercial vessels serving terminals upriver from Philadelphia. Its movable span allows larger ships to pass through the crossing. The incident comes amid heightened scrutiny of vessel collision risks at U.S. bridges following the March 2024 collapse of Baltimore’s Francis Scott Key Bridge, which killed six workers after being struck by the containership Dali . In March 2025, the National Transportation Safety Board identified 68 bridges across 19 states requiring vulnerability assessments, warning that the Baltimore bridge’s risk of collapse from a vessel strike had been nearly 30 times the acceptable threshold for critical bridges. The findings raised broader concerns about whether aging bridge infrastructure is adequately protected against collisions with large commercial vessels. The cause of the incident remains under investigation. Authorities have not reported whether the collision resulted in any restrictions on commercial vessel movements along the Delaware River. REUTERS/Anton Vaganov/File Photo By Bloomberg News Nov 13, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Russia’s October revenues from crude and petroleum-product exports hit the highest since May as the ongoing Iran war bolstered oil prices, according to the International Energy Agency. Russian oil producers earned almost $21.2 billion in export revenue last month, up about 65% from a year earlier, the IEA said in a report Friday. Crude accounted for more than 80% of the total, as the nation’s petroleum-product output and exports were pressured by Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries. The country’s key crude blends, Urals and ESPO, topped $100 a barrel last month due to hostilities in the Middle East, with near daily attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and intense strikes by Houthis on Saudi energy infrastructure, the agency said. That supported demand for Russian barrels, which don’t need to cross Hormuz to reach China and India, their main buyers. Prices above $100 were a welcome development for Russia’s budget, which gets about a fifth of its revenue from the oil and gas industry and which has been strained by the cost of the invasion of Ukraine and sustaining the nation’s wartime economy. The full-year budget deficit is expected to reach 3.2% of gross domestic product this year, government data published Tuesday show. The federal budget doesn’t receive oil revenues directly from exports, but rather through taxing producers, while offering generous subsidies to the industry at the same time. Last month, net budget revenues from oil levies totaled around $10 billion, dented by multi-billion-ruble payouts to support domestic fuel deliveries, Bloomberg calculations based on Finance Ministry data show. Read More: Russia Refinery Payouts Hit Highest Since 2022 in Blow to Budget Russia’s crude oil exports in October remained flat month-on-month at 5.33 million barrels per day, roughly 4% above last year’s level, according to the IEA report. Petroleum-product exports reached 1.49 million barrels per day, the highest since June, though were about a third below the year-earlier level. Ukrainian drone attacks in the first half of October impacted Russian refinery runs, before easing later in the month as Kyiv paused strikes for two weeks. The lull coincided with calls for calm from US President Donald Trump as he sought to bring down fuel prices before the midterm elections. Ukraine has since resumed targeting some of Russia’s key oil refineries, including export-focused plants as Kirishi, and the nation’s largest facility in Omsk. The renewed campaign has already hurt Russian refinery runs, and may lead to higher seaborne crude exports this month, unless Russia’s crude-export terminals are affected. Singapore also remained the world’s largest bunkering port, with marine fuel sales reaching a record 56.77 million tonnes. articles.body: Singapore-Registered Bulk Carrier Strikes US Bridge, Disrupts Traffic Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 The Tacony-Palmyra Bridge spanning the Delaware River between Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and Palmyra, New Jersey, pictured in June 2010 (Credit: Jag9889 / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0) The Singapore-registered bulk carrier STRATEGIC ALLIANCE has struck the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge over the Delaware River between Pennsylvania and New Jersey, forcing a temporary closure before vehicle traffic was partially restored. The incident occurred shortly after 1 p.m. local time on November 12 during a bridge opening for marine traffic, according to the Burlington County Bridge Commission. Representative Ed Neilson reported that the bridge was initially unable to close following the collision, causing significant traffic congestion on the Philadelphia side. The bridge was closed to motorists and pedestrians while officials investigated potential structural damage. Subsequent inspections indicated that the bridge was safe and that the damage appeared minor, the commission said. By 8:40 p.m., two lanes had reopened to motor vehicles, one in each direction, although another lane remained closed for repairs to the pedestrian sidewalk. Pedestrian access to the bridge remained prohibited. Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) confirmed that STRATEGIC ALLIANCE was involved in the incident, reporting no injuries to civilians or crew members, no major damage to the vessel and no marine pollution. The bulk carrier is safely moored at the Kinder Morgan terminal in Pennsylvania, according to MPA. The Singaporean authority said it was in contact with the vessel's management company and relevant US authorities to establish the circumstances of the incident and would conduct an investigation. Repairs and inspections of the bridge are continuing.

November 13, 2026 (Credit: Seaway7) Seaway7 has installed the first inter-array cable at Ørsted's 2.9 GW Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm in the UK North Sea, marking the start of a major cable installation campaign. The company will transport and install more than 536 kilometers of 66kV inter-array cables, connecting the wind turbines to offshore converter stations, Seaway7 announced on November 12. The scope covers 197 inter-array cables at Hornsea 3, which Seaway7 expects to become the world's largest offshore wind farm when completed. The project is the third in Ørsted's Hornsea offshore wind zone for which Seaway7 has secured an inter-array cable installation contract. The company previously transported and installed 89 cables totaling approximately 170 kilometers at Hornsea 1, followed by 165 cables spanning around 382 kilometers at Hornsea 2. Once the latest campaign is completed, Seaway7 will have installed more than 1,000 kilometers of inter-array cables across the three developments. The Hornsea projects are located approximately 90 - 160 kilometers off the east coast of England, in water depths ranging from around 25 to 75 meters. Delivery of the current installation program is being led from Seaway7's Aberdeen office.

articles.title: From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping
articles.summary: Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida, to become what is...
articles.body: Containers Contributions From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping Splash November 13, 2026 0 3,347 3 minutes read Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida , to become what is expected to be the world’s largest artificial reef. Initial underwater inspections found the vessel upright, approximately 180 feet below the surface. The sinking of the SS United States reminds us that ships can outlive their commercial purpose. Launched in 1951 and entering service in 1952, the SS United States was the pinnacle of post-war American maritime engineering. It held the record as the world’s fastest passenger ship but was withdrawn in 1969 as commercial aviation transformed the economics of transatlantic travel. It was not poor engineering that made the ship obsolete, it was a market that had moved on. After decades moored in Philadelphia, the vessel was acquired by Okaloosa County in a project valued at approximately $13m. Its new role will support tourism, marine conservation and research. Its retirement offers a useful perspective on container shipping as it now faces another turning point. A substantial wave of new capacity The container shipping industry is preparing for a significant increase in fleet capacity. According to Drewry’s third-quarter 2026 Container Forecaster the global containership orderbook stood at approximately 13.9m teu on 1 September 2026, equivalent to 40.9% of the active fleet. Drewry forecasts fleet growth of 8.4% in 2027, rising to 12.1% in 2028 before moderating to 9.4% in 2029. The concern is the market into which these ships will be delivered. During the pandemic, congestion, equipment shortages and route disruption absorbed vessel capacity. Diversions around the Cape of Good Hope lengthened voyages and tied up ships. Carriers responded by ordering larger, more fuel-efficient vessels anticipating continued trade growth, but shipbuilding schedules are long and in the era of the never normal, market conditions change quickly. If Red Sea and Suez Canal routings return progressively to normal, shorter voyages could release significant effective capacity without a single additional ship entering service. Combined with newbuildings, this could widen the gap between supply and demand. Vessel capacity could potentially reach as much as 10% above demand under such circumstances. The consequences could include lower freight rates, tougher competition for cargo, blank sailings, slower steaming, vessel idling and accelerated recycling of older tonnage. The industry faces a major capacity-management challenge. The cost of getting the timing wrong Aviation permanently changed the market for passenger liners, while container shipping remains essential to trade. New vessels will not automatically become redundant. Nevertheless, ships are long-term capital investments, ordered years before delivery and expected to earn returns over operating lives spanning decades. A vessel ordered when freight rates are high and capacity constrained may enter service when demand is weaker, transit times are shorter and competing tonnage is plentiful. Efficiency alone cannot guarantee a satisfactory return. Carriers will have to decide which vessels to deploy, which trades to prioritise and when to redeploy or retire older ships. Smaller vessels displaced from mainline routes may move into regional trades, adding competitive pressure whilst others may be laid up, sold or recycled. Ports and terminals may see service patterns, berth requirements and transhipment flows change. Shippers may welcome lower rates but carriers protecting utilisation may consolidate services, withdraw sailings or alter port rotations. Lower prices could therefore come with less predictable frequency and transit times. The costs of poor capacity planning will ultimately ripple through businesses to end users and consumers. A different future for ageing vessels The SS United States project raises the question of what happens when ships lose their original commercial purpose. Conversion into an artificial reef offers a potential tourism and conservation role but it is neither a universal nor necessarily economical solution for commercial vessels. For surplus container ships, recycling will remain the principal end-of-life option when redeployment is no longer viable. Some older vessels may serve feeder networks or specialised trades, provided their economics remain competitive. Fleet renewal should consider the economic, environmental and operational consequences of retiring existing tonnage and not just the efficiency gains promised by newbuildings. The SS United States was a remarkable engineering achievement but it could not escape changing transportation economics. Its story reminds us that a ship’s commercial lifespan is determined not simply by how well it is built but by whether the market still needs what it does. As the industry approaches 2027, the question is whether carriers have ordered more capacity than the market can sustainably absorb and how prepared they are to manage the consequences. The challenge is not simply to build the next generation of vessels. It is to ensure there is a commercially sustainable reason to put them to work. It’s not something we as an industry have a good track doing. articles.body: Oil Heads for Weekly Decline Despite Middle East Supply Threats Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 © Miha Creative / Adobe Stock Oil prices edged up on Friday but were headed for a second weekly decline as the continued US focus on its blockade and economic pressure on Iran eased fears of renewed fighting in the Middle East, though shipping attacks remained a supply risk. Brent futures LCOc1 were up 53 cents, or 0.55%, to $96.35 a barrel at 0900 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures CLc1 added 20 cents, or 0.23%, to $88.94 a barrel. For the week, Brent and WTI were both on track for a 2% drop. The benchmarks plunged 16% and 13%, respectively, last week. "The market is range bound post midterms. The ability for more hostilities (in Iran) is restricted but a deal is equally elusive," said Jeff Currie, founder of Real Macro and former global head of commodities research at Goldman Sachs. "That means the market is roughly balanced, with the ability to trade up limited and the ability to trade down limited," he said. Oil has had a volatile trading week, with earlier hopes for a rapprochement in the US-Israeli war on Iran, now in its ninth month, offset by strikes on Saudi Arabian infrastructure by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and attacks on tankers shipping crude out of the Gulf. US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social a deal with Iran was not necessary to end the war. "Trump's indications that further military escalation against Iran may not be necessary have raised expectations that Washington could increasingly rely on economic sanctions and restrictions on oil shipments rather than intensifying military operations," said Sugandha Sachdeva, founder of SS WealthStreet, a New Delhi-based research firm. The weakness in oil prices is also largely driven by signs of softening US demand, as rising crude oil and fuel inventories indicate a relatively subdued consumption outlook, Sachdeva said. US crude and fuel inventories rose last week, driven by softer refined products demand and a jump in oil imports, the Energy Information Administration said on Thursday. Despite the easing prices, risks remain for oil shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway for crude exports from the main Middle East producers. On Thursday, Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not immediately verify the Iranian accounts. That same day, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked a pumping station on the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, an oil facility in the Saudi Red Sea city of Yanbu, and an Aramco building in the capital Riyadh. "Geopolitical risks remain elevated, and any fresh disruption to oil supplies could quickly reignite upward pressure on prices," Sachdeva of SS WealthStreet said. (Reuters - Reporting by Anna Hirtenstein in London. Additional reporting by Helen Clark and Sethuraman N R; Editing by Christian Schmollinger, Sonali Paul, Thomas Derpinghaus and Tomasz Janowski)

The measures also cover nine companies, including Russian oil producer Slavneft, Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project and several energy trading businesses based in Dubai. The latest vessel additions include LNG carriers Melicertes, Neleus, Perle, Aeolus and Oneiroi , alongside the Novatek-linked Koryak FSU . On the oil side, London has blacklisted Apeks, Sara Sky, Balu 6, Yvika and Alma . The vessels operate under a mix of Russian, Panamanian, Sierra Leonean and Djiboutian flags, according to the official sanctions notice. The restrictions prohibit the specified ships from accessing British ports and impose controls on chartering and operating them. They also restrict the provision of services including ship finance, broking, technical assistance and crewing, subject to applicable exceptions and licensing arrangements. The corporate additions extend the crackdown beyond individual ships. Dubai-based Forteza Trading, Patera and Novus Energy have been designated, with British authorities specifically linking Novus Energy to dealings involving vessels already subject to UK restrictions. Russian petrochemical producer Sibur and coal groups SUEK and Kuzbassrazrezugol also feature in the latest package. The move brings all ten of Russia’s largest oil producers under British sanctions following the inclusion of Slavneft. The government announced the measures during the European Political Community summit in Dublin, where pressure on Russian energy revenues formed part of discussions on Ukraine. Britain has been steadily expanding its maritime restrictions this year, including sanctions against six ships in August and an earlier package targeting Russia’s developing LNG shadow fleet. articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables Deutsche Windtechnik picked for UK offshore wind maintenance job Bojan Lepic November 13, 2026 0 410 1 minute read UK Government UK Government German offshore wind services specialist Deutsche Windtechnik has secured a five-year operations and maintenance contract covering two offshore wind farms in the UK. The agreement, awarded by asset manager XceCo, covers the Lynn and Inner Dowsing wind farms off Lincolnshire, which have a combined installed capacity of 194.4MW. The contract will begin on April 1, 2027, and covers all 54 turbines across the two projects. According to Deutsche Windtechnik, the agreement represents the first full-scope UK offshore wind service contract awarded to an independent provider. The two adjacent wind farms, located approximately 5 km off Skegness, entered operation in 2009 and comprise 27 turbines each. The assets are wholly owned by funds managed by Macquarie Asset Management, which increased its ownership from 60.75% to 100% in 2024. The projects have historically operated under a self-perform maintenance model overseen by XceCo. Under the new arrangement, Deutsche Windtechnik will assume responsibility for integrated maintenance services, while XceCo retains its asset management role. Preparations for the transition are already underway, including technical and operational handover, workforce integration and the transfer of operating processes and systems. The contract adds to Deutsche Windtechnik’s growing offshore wind maintenance portfolio. articles.title: Gulf war leaves toxic legacy that could last decades
articles.summary: Greenpeace has identified 540 possible oil spills across the Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Sea since the US-Iran war began on February 28 (see map below), with satellite imagery showing a cumulative slick footprint of approximately 20,000 sq km. Not all detections have been conclusively linked to attacks on...
articles.body: Environment Middle East Tankers Gulf war leaves toxic legacy that could last decades Sam Chambers November 13, 2026 0 918 2 minutes read CENTCOM CENTCOM Greenpeace has identified 540 possible oil spills across the Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Sea since the US-Iran war began on February 28 (see map below), with satellite imagery showing a cumulative slick footprint of approximately 20,000 sq km. Not all detections have been conclusively linked to attacks on shipping. The environmental consequences could last for decades. A 2022 study published in the Journal of Marine Science and Engineering found extensive oil deposits along more than 25 km of Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island coastline, almost 40 years after the 1983–85 Nowruz oil spills during the Iran-Iraq war. Researchers found oil contamination in 76% of 1,434 test pits, demonstrating how petroleum residues can persist long after surface slicks disappear. The spills continue daily with many more strikes on ships being reported every week. Iran has claimed that four oil tankers struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz over the past two days, while a separately confirmed attack on a Sinokor-operated tanker off the United Arab Emirates forced the evacuation of 22 seafarers. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed yesterday that two supertankers carrying more than 4m barrels of oil between them had been disabled by explosions on Wednesday after ignoring warnings against using what Tehran described as an unauthorised route through the strait. Iranian state media attributed the explosions to naval mines and broadcast footage purporting to show the incidents. The Iranian army subsequently claimed that another two tankers struck mines in the eastern part of the strait on Thursday afternoon after ignoring navigation warnings and switching off their radar systems. None of the four vessels has been identified, and the claims have not been independently verified. Separately, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed that a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, at 1800 GMT on Wednesday. The projectile hit the vessel’s engine room, starting a fire and forcing the evacuation of its crew. India’s shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal subsequently identified the vessel as the Liberia-flagged Dominica Prosperity, reporting that all 22 crew members, including 19 Indian nationals, had been safely evacuated. The tanker was drifting off Mina Saqr when the attack occurred. The International Maritime Organization’s latest tally of Hormuz strikes, covering incidents confirmed through November 11, stands at 134, with 25 seafarers killed since the conflict began in late February. articles.title: Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial
articles.summary: One of shipping’s most consequential legal battles has concluded in London, with the Baltic Exchange and commodities trader Mercuria awaiting a High Court ruling on whether the industry’s leading VLCC freight benchmark should have continued operating after war erupted in the Middle East. The three-week trial ended...
articles.body: Europe Tankers Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial Sam Chambers November 13, 2026 0 895 2 minutes read One of shipping’s most consequential legal battles has concluded in London, with the Baltic Exchange and commodities trader Mercuria awaiting a High Court ruling on whether the industry’s leading VLCC freight benchmark should have continued operating after war erupted in the Middle East. The three-week trial ended yesterday, with judgment expected to take several months. At the centre of the dispute is TD3C, the Baltic’s benchmark for transporting crude from Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia to Ningbo, China, a voyage requiring passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Mercuria has argued that the disruption following the outbreak of hostilities on February 28 rendered the benchmark unreliable, with insufficient physical tanker activity to support meaningful assessments. The trading house maintains that the Baltic failed to meet its statutory and contractual obligations by continuing to publish rates despite mounting evidence that its contributing shipbrokers could not reliably determine a market price. During the trial, Mercuria highlighted internal communications revealing considerable uncertainty among Baltic staff and broker panellists. One Baltic assessor reportedly described the rates as “utter nonsense”, while a contributing broker questioned how a market could be assessed when virtually no vessels were fixing voyages. Mercuria also challenged the Baltic’s reliance on forward freight agreement prices when calculating a benchmark that itself underpins derivatives contracts, raising concerns about circular pricing. However, the trader significantly narrowed its case during closing arguments, abandoning demands for retrospective invalidation or suspension of the index. The Baltic, owned by the Singapore Exchange, has vigorously rejected the allegations, arguing that its established methodology remained appropriate despite extraordinary market conditions. Its lawyers maintain that experienced shipbrokers could still assess freight values using available market intelligence, including transactions, vessel movements and derivatives pricing. The exchange also pointed to continuing vessel transits through Hormuz during the disputed period, disputing Mercuria’s contention that there was no meaningful underlying market. In closing arguments, the Baltic accused Mercuria of repeatedly changing its case and suggested the litigation was an attempt to escape the consequences of unsuccessful trading positions. Mercuria rejected allegations of wrongdoing. The Baltic has also warned that retrospective intervention in a widely used benchmark could create significant uncertainty for freight derivatives and physical shipping contracts linked to TD3C. The dispute has exposed uncomfortable questions about the governance of shipping’s freight indices, particularly when geopolitical events make conventional market assessments exceptionally difficult. The Baltic Exchange has consistently defended its benchmark procedures and regulatory compliance. Mr Justice Andrew Baker must now determine whether those procedures satisfied the exchange’s obligations during an unprecedented disruption to tanker trading. The implications extend well beyond the two companies, potentially influencing how freight benchmarks are maintained during future market emergencies. articles.title: New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping
articles.summary: Hong Kong Maritime Week is about to kick off. To celebrate the occasion, Splash today publishes a 48-page magazine on the city’s maritime hub credentials. A ship can be ordered at a mainland Chinese yard, owned through a leasing company in Hong Kong, insured in London, crewed through a management operation in Asia...
articles.body: Contributions Greater China New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping Splash November 13, 2026 0 1,585 8 minutes read Hong Kong Maritime Week is about to kick off. To celebrate the occasion, Splash today publishes a 48-page magazine on the city’s maritime hub credentials. A ship can be ordered at a mainland Chinese yard, owned through a leasing company in Hong Kong, insured in London, crewed through a management operation in Asia and chartered from Singapore. Its cargo need never pass through Hong Kong’s harbour. Even its Hong Kong financing vehicle may have to seek credit approval elsewhere. The geography of shipping has always been complicated. What has changed is the urgency with which Hong Kong must ask where the real business takes place. Is the city still a maritime capital in its own right, chosen by international owners, traders and financiers because of what it offers? Or is it becoming a highly sophisticated services counter for the vast industrial and commercial machine next door? On paper, the answer looks reassuring. Hong Kong remains fourth in the 2026 Xinhua-Baltic international maritime centre rankings, behind Singapore, Shanghai and London. Three of the world’s leading shipmanagement companies are headquartered here, major P&I clubs operate here, and the city retains a formidable concentration of lawyers, financiers and technical expertise. Look towards the waterfront, however, and a different picture emerges. The container port handled 12.99m teu in 2025, scarcely half its 2008 peak. The register has shed substantial tonnage amid geopolitical upheaval, falling to 109m gt by June this year. Shanghai, Shenzhen and Guangzhou have grown into maritime giants whose physical advantages Hong Kong cannot realistically overturn. These are not contradictory stories. Together they define the central question running through this special report: whether Hong Kong can convert its inherited maritime strengths into a sustainable business model for 2030, even as its traditional measures of importance become less flattering. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, resists the suggestion that the city is being reduced to an adjunct of the mainland. “An ‘annex’ does not host three of the world’s top 10 shipmanagers, 11 of the 12 International Group P&I associations, eight of the top ten ship-finance bookrunners,” he says, pointing also to the city’s legal institutions and international industry organisations. This inventory represents decades of investment and commercial trust. Yet it does not settle the more difficult question of what those institutions actually do here, or whether their next expansion will take place somewhere else. Where the decisions are made Hong Kong has spent much of this decade making itself more attractive on tax. Qualifying ship lessors can enjoy a zero profits-tax rate; eligible ship leasing managers, shipmanagers, agents and brokers benefit from half-rate treatment, as do certain marine insurers. The administration has also sought to broaden the proposition to physical commodity traders, recognising that traders create demand for chartering, insurance, finance and legal services The first results are tangible, but open to interpretation. Government figures show the number of ship leasing enterprises under the relevant preferential regime rising from 11 in 2020/21 to 46 in 2022/23. That is evidence that structures and businesses have responded. It says much less about the location of credit committees, the people selecting vessels or the teams negotiating charters. “Tax is necessary but not sufficient,” Hext says. Companies, he argues, follow customers, skills, capital and regulatory certainty. He wants the next phase judged by “regional headquarters, underwriting authority, credit decisions, trading desks and skilled jobs, and not by company registrations alone”. Gautam Chellaram, chairman of KC Maritime, is more sceptical about what tax reform has delivered. He sees genuine growth in leasing and mainland-linked finance, but says: “I do not yet see clear evidence that the measures have resulted in substantial headquarters relocation involving decision-makers, fund managers, and independent shipowners physically basing themselves in Hong Kong.” It would be equally wrong to dismiss the developments as bookkeeping. Hong Kong is a place where ships are managed, risks assessed and capital arranged, not merely where documents are signed. Dockendale Group is among the companies expanding management operations locally. Its chief executive, Vikrant Gusain, says Hong Kong’s ease of doing business is an important factor in the decision, alongside access to Asian markets and international talent. The competitive comparison nevertheless remains Singapore. “Singapore continues to offer broader tax incentives and a larger concentration of commodity traders,” says Jim James, senior consultant at Hill Dickinson. The latter point may be more important than the former. Traders and charterers bring transactions, and transactions bring the brokers, lenders, insurers and lawyers who serve them. A critical mass of principals is extraordinarily difficult to manufacture through concessions alone. Hong Kong has distinct advantages of its own. Its banking network connects Chinese and international capital; its offshore renminbi role creates opportunities for trade and leasing; and its links with a vast manufacturing and shipbuilding hinterland provide access that a competing maritime centre cannot reproduce. But geographical proximity is not the same thing as commercial gravity. The city must persuade companies to put people with mandates and budgets here, not just a local subsidiary. June’s tax amendment bill, including a proposed half-rate concession for qualifying physical commodity trading, gives the policy another push. September’s first five-year plan adds a ‘Finance + Maritime’ agenda built around ship finance, insurance, trade finance and related services. Neither initiative can be called successful solely because it exists. Their test will be new trading desks, lending decisions and customers with genuine freedom to transact elsewhere. The mainland advantage — and the danger Where does this leave the argument that Hong Kong is becoming Shanghai’s professional-services annex? Chellaram offers the report’s most uncomfortable formulation: as a cargo port, the city is being functionally subordinated to mainland competitors, but as a financial, legal and arbitration centre it retains qualities not available in the same combination across the border. “On the professional-services side, Hong Kong is the piece Shanghai structurally cannot replicate,” he says. The separate customs territory, common-law system, freely convertible currency and established international business practices all give the city a distinctive purpose. The opportunity is to sell those qualities to the world, not simply to companies moving through China. Damien Laracy, partner and head of Hill Dickinson’s Hong Kong office, describes a transition “from a cargo-driven port hub to a specialised centre for maritime services”. Rather than an annex, he sees “the region’s high-value maritime services platform, complementing the manufacturing, cargo, and port capacity of neighbouring cities”. The distinction is subtle but critical. A law firm advising a mainland shipowner on a vessel financing can be doing genuine international business from Hong Kong. So can an insurer handling a casualty thousands of miles away or a manager overseeing a fleet trading between Brazil and India. But the city’s position becomes more vulnerable if its principal attraction is merely that it makes mainland transactions easier. The international test is whether owners and counterparties with no direct mainland connection still choose Hong Kong. The machinery of a genuine maritime centre is already here. English-language maritime contracts, established common-law precedents, internationally recognised arbitration and access to mainland enforcement arrangements give it a credible offering. Rosita Lau, a partner at Ince, is among those urging the city to promote its legal and dispute-resolution capabilities far more systematically. The fact that Hong Kong can be chosen in a contract is not proof that it will be. There are also more prosaic measures of legal competitiveness. Martyn Huckerby, head of competition law and regulatory at Hill Dickinson, points to the extension of the block exemption for liner vessel-sharing agreements to 2031. The renewal, he says, preserves “legal certainty for operational cooperation between liner shipping companies”. It is a narrow regulatory decision, but one of the many predictable rules on which internationally mobile businesses build long-term operations. Insurance offers another illustration of integration without inevitable subordination. London P&I has served shipowners from Hong Kong for decades and opened an office in Shanghai in 2025. Deborah Yu, its regional director for Asia, says the two offices work together with the club’s operations in London and Athens. The point is not to force every Asian insurance decision into Hong Kong, but to ensure the city continues to handle work that could plausibly be located elsewhere. International outlook An international city must keep choosing to be international. That means foreign owners can operate comfortably, specialist staff can build careers and global counterparties can trust their contracts, information and capital to an environment they understand. This issue explores what that requirement means in practice. Hong Kong’s shipmanagement concentration provides a genuine strategic asset: it would take years to reproduce the crewing, technical and training networks that leading managers have built here. The challenge is keeping enough experienced people to make decisions locally as digitalisation, alternative fuels and increasingly complex compliance change the skill set. The same logic applies to finance and insurance. An internationally recognised logo on a Hong Kong office does not tell us whether it can approve a ship loan or underwrite a specialist risk. A registry’s gross tonnage does not establish where the family that owns the ship runs its business. A port’s box count says little about the value of transactions governed by local law, but the loss of container activity cannot be waved away simply by relabelling the city a services centre. Technology adds a further test. Hong Kong’s Port Community System is meant to help connect cargo movements, documentation and financing across the supply chain. But common platforms are only as useful as the trust and security behind them. Paul Haswell, technology partner at Hill Dickinson, notes that digitisation will bring “increased emphasis on data security and the monitoring of systems”. A financial and logistics crossroads cannot afford to treat cyber resilience as an optional extra. The city’s new maritime ambitions, particularly green bunkering and transition finance, depend on the same mixture of hard infrastructure and intangible trust. There is little value in promoting alternative fuels unless ships can take them safely, on schedule and at competitive prices. There is little point marketing green ship finance unless lenders and owners are prepared to commit capital against realistic assumptions about technology, fuel availability and earnings. Government has clearly recognised the need to change. Its first five-year plan shifts the emphasis from volume to value, promising stronger maritime services, a greener and smarter port, closer links with the Greater Bay Area and a more developed marine finance ecosystem. The question is no longer whether officials have ambitions. It is whether businesses can see projects proceeding quickly enough, and with sufficient commercial substance, to justify staying and expanding. That demands a sharper understanding of competition. Singapore can be a partner and a rival. Shanghai can be a customer, collaborator and competitor. The Greater Bay Area can supply Hong Kong with enormous commercial opportunities while simultaneously taking cargo, talent and investment from it. Those apparently inconsistent propositions are the reality of a maritime industry in which business moves wherever the overall proposition is strongest. The defensible future is neither a nostalgic campaign to win back every container nor a comfortable acceptance of being the mainland’s legal and financial back office. It is a city that remains indispensable to international shipping because substantive work is done there: ships are managed, cargo is traded, capital is committed, risks are insured and disputes are resolved. By 2030, Hong Kong should be judged less by how many companies have an address in Central or how many development plans have been published, and more by who has authority to do business from the city. Are the next fleet acquisitions decided here? Are traders locating profitable operations here? Are international parties choosing Hong Kong law when they have no obligation to do so? Are young maritime professionals staying because the best opportunities are available here? A gateway is somewhere business passes through. A maritime capital is somewhere business chooses to stay. Hong Kong has spent generations proving it can be both. The coming four years will show whether it still can. You can read the magazine ahead of Hong Kong Maritime Week by clicking here .
